title: Relief work
hookLine: Taiwanese Buddhist relief volunteers at disasters around the world

cards: A line of volunteers in navy blue and white moves through a town after an earthquake, carrying blankets, rice and hot meals.
When one of them hands a blanket to an old man, she uses both hands, then bows to him and says thank you. Not you're welcome. Thank you.
The man looks surprised: why is the giver thanking him? That small bow belongs to a Buddhist relief movement from Taiwan, one that tells its own beginning as a handful of coins.

teach.b: First, the founder. The movement is called Tzu Chi, which its members translate as compassion and relief. It was founded by a Buddhist nun, Dharma Master Cheng Yen, on Taiwan's east coast.

teach.h: A COIN IN A BAMBOO TUBE.
teach.b: The story the movement tells goes like this: she asked a small group of housewives to drop a little coin into a bamboo tube each day, before going to market, to help the poor. A small amount, they asked?
Small, she said, but every day. Tradition says that's how it started: not with a big gift but with a daily one.
The coins grew into clinics, hospitals and teams of volunteers that now travel to floods, earthquakes and storms far beyond Taiwan. Third, the giving itself.
In Buddhism giving is called dana, a practice anyone can start with.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "let him overcome the greedy by liberality." Tzu Chi volunteers add a twist.
They thank the person who receives, because receiving gives the volunteer a chance to practice. Hence the bow. Fourth, what it asks of the volunteer.
Volunteers include ordinary lay people: shopkeepers, teachers, retirees. They clean mud out of houses, cook in field kitchens and sort recycling to raise funds.
As the movement sees it, the work is the practice: not a reward, not a good deed to boast about.
Hands that help, and a mind that stays humble while they do it.

how: Tzu Chi volunteers, founded around the nun Cheng Yen in Taiwan, bring food, shelter and medical care after disasters, often handing aid with both hands and thanking those who receive it.

games.q: you're a volunteer after an earthquake. you hand an old man a blanket. what do you say?
games.why: Tzu Chi volunteers thank the one who receives: his need gave them a chance to practice giving.

practice: Open your hands on your knees, palms up, and let one place that's hurting right now come to mind, after a flood, a fire, a quake or a war.

Think of one way you could give, even a little, the way the housewives gave a coin; if money isn't possible, think of time, or a word passed on to someone who can. Then sit with the idea of thanking the people you help.

wordCard.voice: Relief work. Buddhist volunteers bringing food, shelter and care after disasters, treating giving as practice and thanking those who receive. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit dana: giving, generosity, the practice behind every blanket and meal.

carryVoice: Your line: hands that help. A coin a day, and a bow for the one who receives. See you tomorrow.
